title: Corgi — AI-Native Full-Stack Insurance Carrier Hits $1.3B Unicorn Valuation Four Months After Series A
author: Dominic-Madori Davis · Duncan Riley

dom.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem

mo.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
AI services: Deployment gaps create consulting opportunity
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

kp.k: AI-native carrier integrates regulated insurance operations
kp.d: SiliconANGLE reports that Corgi obtained regulatory approval as a licensed carrier in July 2025 and runs underwriting, policy management and claims in-house using AI. The reported model delivers insurance itself rather than merely supplying software to incumbent providers; Corgi describes itself as the first AI-native, full-stack insurance platform purpose-built for startups.
qs: The company won regulatory approval as a licensed carrier in July 2025.

Its AI systems run underwriting, policy management and claims in-house, instead of stitching together work across the third-party administrators, managing general agents, reinsurers and carriers that handle most of these functions at established insurers.

kp.k: Integration promises faster quoting and adaptable coverage
kp.d: Corgi argues that owning the full stack and applying AI to core workflows overcomes fragmented legacy infrastructure. SiliconANGLE attributes to the company a platform that analyzes thousands of company, industry and risk-profile data points to quote in under 10 minutes, with policies typically bound the same day rather than two to four weeks. These are reported operational claims, not results from an independent comparative study.
qs: Corgi argues that owning the full stack and applying AI to core workflows produces quicker quoting, more adaptive risk models and coverage that can be adjusted in something closer to real time.
Under the hood, Corgi says, its platform analyzes thousands of data points about a company, its industry and its risk profile to generate quotes in under 10 minutes.
Policies are typically bound the same day rather than the two to four weeks more common at legacy carriers.

kp.k: AI absorbs workflows previously distributed across intermediaries
kp.d: SiliconANGLE describes Corgi's operating mechanism as removing the broker layer while acting as carrier, issuing coverage, managing claims and maintaining its own policy administration system. AI handles much of the workflow traditionally passed among brokers, administrators and underwriters; the document does not quantify staffing reductions or specify the extent of human supervision.
qs: The idea is that by cutting out the broker layer and operating as the carrier itself, Corgi underwrites policies, issues coverage, manages claims and runs its own policy administration system in-house.
AI handles much of the workflow that traditionally moves among brokers, third-party administrators and underwriters.

kp.k: AI liability becomes a distinct insurance product
kp.d: SiliconANGLE reports an AI liability product paired with existing technology errors and omissions insurance, marketed against losses from biased algorithms, harmful or inaccurate generated content, training-data misuse, adversarial attacks, synthetic media and autonomous-system failures. Laqua argues that legacy policies exclude or ambiguously address these risks. These are descriptions of product positioning and company claims, not analysis of policy wording or adjudicated coverage.
qs: Corgi has also recently added an AI liability product that pairs with a customer's existing technology errors and omissions policy.

The AI coverage is pitched as protection against losses tied to biased algorithms, harmful or inaccurate generated content, misuse of training data, adversarial attacks on models, synthetic media and autonomous system failures.
Many legacy policies either exclude these risks or handle them ambiguously.

kp.k: Modular insurance targets startups’ changing needs
kp.d: The reports identify startups as Corgi's principal market and name Deel and Artisan as customers. SiliconANGLE lists directors and officers, errors and omissions, cyber, commercial general liability, hired and non-owned auto, and fiduciary liability coverage. Dashboard-based modular policies are intended to let customers adjust coverage around fundraising, hiring and larger enterprise contracts.
qs: Standard startup coverages on offer include directors and officers liability, errors and omissions liability, cyber, commercial general liability, hired and non-owned auto and fiduciary liability.
Coverage is offered on a modular basis, so customers can add or upgrade policies from a dashboard when they raise a round, hire their first non-founder employee, or sign a larger enterprise contract.

kp.k: Funding accelerates alongside ambitious expansion plans
kp.d: TechCrunch's 6 May report records a TCV-led $160 million Series B at a $1.3 billion valuation, four months after a $108 million Series A, with total funding stated as $268 million. Its 28 May report records a $106 million Series B1 at $2.6 billion and states total funding of $378 million. SiliconANGLE's 6 May account instead says more than $268 million had been raised. The document supplies these totals without reconciling them.
qs: This comes just four months after the company announced a $108 million Series A. The company has now raised $268 million in funding to date, Laqua said, and has become Y Combinator's latest unicorn.

Insurance tech Corgi on Thursday announced a $106 million Series B1 raise, valuing the company at $2.6 billion, just three weeks after announcing a $160 million Series B at a $1.3 billion valuation and four months after its $108 million Series A.
Corgi has now raised $378 million in total funding from its investors.
The new funding takes the total raised by Corgi to more than $268 million.

kp.k: Capital supports underwriting, distribution and new verticals
kp.d: SiliconANGLE reports that Corgi began in property management insurance and is expanding toward trucking, with payroll and small business identified as future areas. Laqua attributes the additional financing to insurance's capital intensity, accelerated demand across products and partnerships, and the costs of building an AI-native platform. Planned uses include new insurance categories, AI underwriting, embedded distribution and team growth; these are management plans and explanations rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: It is also moving into new industries, with trucking the first target outside its initial market. Payroll and small business coverage are flagged as future areas of expansion.
When asked about the back-to-back rounds, Laqua said that insurance is a "highly capital-intensive industry," and that "demand has accelerated quickly across new product lines and partnerships."

"We're best known for our business insurance products, but the additional capital will be used to expand into new insurance categories, scale the AI underwriting platform, grow embedded distribution partnerships, and continue growing our team," Laqua said.

kp.k: Rapid valuation doubling raises venture-markup concerns
kp.d: TechCrunch's 28 May article questions the three-week valuation doubling, particularly because it reports the same investor set in both rounds. An anonymous limited partner expresses broader distrust of internal markups without liquidity events. Kindred Ventures investor Kanyi Maqubela counters that company momentum and revenue growth justified the round and says limited partners discount markups. No revenue figures are supplied to substantiate that explanation.
qs: While startups raising back-to-back rounds at steep step-ups have become almost routine, a company whose valuation doubles in three weeks is unusual enough to raise questions, particularly given the investor set in both rounds is the same.
The specific concern is that a fund that invests at one valuation, then marks it up three weeks later can make portfolio performance look stronger on paper than the underlying business may justify.
They discount the value of markups since those aren't always reflective of reality.
He added that in this case, revenue growth rationalized the new round.

kp.k: Legal relevance is explicitly a cross-domain analogy
kp.d: The document's editorial relevance section, rather than the underlying insurance reporting, frames Corgi as a comparator for AI-native legal providers owning regulated delivery and core operations instead of selling tools to incumbents. It draws parallels to Manifest OS, Carta Law and Kirkland, and compares funding velocity with Harvey, Legora, Eve and EvenUp. The same section cautions against interpreting venture valuation increases as measures of business performance.
qs: Corgi is an **out-of-domain comparator**, included to sharpen the AI-native-vertical argument.

The structural analogue to legal: an AI-native entrant that owns the entire regulated stack (carrier licence plus AI-run core operations) rather than selling tools to incumbents — parallel to Manifest OS owning its law firms, Carta Law absorbing legal into its ERP, and Kirkland building proprietary AI to own its stack.

The 28 May piece is worth carrying alongside the 6 May one precisely because it supplies the counterweight: TechCrunch's own reporting treats the three-week doubling as a question about venture marking practice, not as a measure of the business.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Corgi claims that integrating AI with a licensed, full-stack insurance carrier automates fragmented insurance workflows and makes coverage faster and more adaptable.
pts.d: In SiliconANGLE's 6 May 2026 reporting, Duncan Riley attributes to Corgi the argument that owning the carrier and its operating systems allows AI to run underwriting, policy management and claims in-house, rather than distributing work across intermediaries. The claimed benefits are quicker quotes, more adaptive risk models and coverage adjustments closer to real time. Riley describes AI as handling much of the workflow, not necessarily all work without human supervision. This is an insurance-domain claim, not evidence of changes in legal services.

pts.k: Corgi presents AI-related liabilities as a market for insurance coverage that legacy policies may exclude or address ambiguously.
pts.d: In Dominic-Madori Davis's 28 May TechCrunch article, co-founder Nico Laqua claims Corgi covers financial loss, misinformation, operational failures and compliance issues caused by AI. Riley's 6 May account describes a recently added AI liability product paired with an existing technology errors and omissions policy, pitched to address algorithmic bias, generated-content harms, training-data misuse, adversarial attacks, synthetic media and autonomous-system failures. These are descriptions of marketed coverage, not findings about how particular claims have been paid or policy exclusions interpreted.

pts.k: Corgi's founders plan to extend AI-enabled operations into additional insurance categories and industries using new capital.
pts.d: Riley reports plans to broaden products and distribution and invest further in underwriting and claims AI, with trucking the first target outside the initial market and payroll and small business identified as future expansion areas. Co-founder Emily Yuan describes this as automating difficult real-economy workflows. In the 28 May article, Laqua identifies scaling the AI underwriting platform, embedded distribution partnerships and team growth as uses of the additional funding. These are corporate intentions rather than demonstrated expansion outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The operational claims rely chiefly on company descriptions, including quantitative turnaround claims, rather than independent performance evaluation.
pts.d: Riley reports that Corgi received carrier regulatory approval in July 2025 and attributes to the company a platform that analyzes thousands of data points and produces quotes in under ten minutes. The article also states that policies are typically bound the same day, against two to four weeks at legacy carriers. No sample, measurement period, comparison methodology, underwriting accuracy, claims-handling results or loss-ratio data are supplied. TechCrunch names Deel and Artisan as customers, but supplies no customer-level outcome evidence. The text offers no independent test separating the effects of AI from those of vertical integration.

pts.k: Funding and valuation provide evidence of financing activity, while the later TechCrunch article explicitly distinguishes valuation markups from underlying business performance.
pts.d: Davis reports a $160 million Series B at a $1.3 billion valuation on 6 May and a $106 million Series B1 at a $2.6 billion valuation on 28 May. Investor Kanyi Maqubela attributes the step-up to momentum and revenue growth, without supplying revenue figures. Laqua cites accelerated demand across product lines and partnerships and the capital intensity of insurance. Davis raises questions about the rapid repricing with the same investor set and quotes an anonymous limited partner's general concern about internal markups; this is not a finding of wrongdoing at Corgi. These reports do not establish AI-driven profitability or operating superiority. The supplied accounts also give inconsistent YC cohort labels, and the stated $378 million total funding is not reconciled with the $374 million sum of the three listed rounds.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Core workflow capabilities are presented as operating by May 2026; broader expansion remains prospective and capital-dependent.
pts.d: The articles describe a company founded in 2024, licensed as a carrier in July 2025 and operating AI-supported insurance workflows by 6 May 2026. Under-ten-minute quoting and typical same-day binding are present-tense claims, not universal guarantees. Near-real-time adjustment is qualified as an approximation. Modular coverage can be added or upgraded when customers raise funding, hire a first non-founder employee or sign a larger enterprise contract. The AI liability product is described as paired with existing technology errors and omissions insurance. Expansion is tied to the new financing, with no completion dates specified.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are startup insurance buyers, insurance intermediaries and incumbents, prospective customers in new sectors, and investors.
pts.d: Startups are presented as underserved buyers that could obtain faster, more adjustable insurance and explicit AI-risk coverage. Brokers, third-party administrators and underwriters perform workflows that Corgi says it internalizes or automates; the source gives no employment-displacement estimates. Legacy carriers are the comparison group for speed and coverage limitations. Property-management customers are the initial market, with trucking, payroll and small business targeted for expansion. Venture investors and their limited partners are affected by the rapid financing and valuation changes. The document's legal-essay relevance section supplies an analogy to AI-native legal providers, but the underlying reporting makes no concrete claims about lawyers, law-firm staffing or legal-service outcomes.
